The folder `data/` holds the data behind a published data story, "NYC's Urban Textscape": https://pudding.cool/2025/07/street-view/
The files: data/terms.csv

Write down the story's findings that this data reproduces.

1. Read the story on the web. web_fetch returns the page as the server sends it. web_view opens it in a browser and scrolls it like a reader, so it also gets text drawn by scripts, chart labels and the text of scrolling steps: use it when web_fetch returns little of the story, and to read what the charts label. Follow links to the story's methods or data notes when they say how a number was computed.
2. List every finding the authors draw from data: each number, comparison, ranking, share, trend or pattern the text states or a chart labels. A description of the data itself is not a finding: how many records, people, items, categories or sources it has, and how it was collected. When a chart states the same thing for each of its items (the top three for each phrase, the share for each year), that is one finding, written as one fact whose code computes it for every item at once.
3. Write each finding the files in data/ can reproduce as a fact in `facts.json`:

```json
[{"id": "women-front-shorter",
  "source": "On average, the pockets in women's jeans are 48% shorter and 6.5% narrower than men's pockets.",
  "claim": "Women's front pockets average 14.3 cm of maximum height against 23.1 cm for men.",
  "tables": {"m": "data/measurements.csv"},
  "code": "m.groupby('menWomen').maxHeightFront.mean()"}]
```

- `id`: unique in the file, a few meaningful words.
- `source`: the story's own words for this finding, quoted exactly, from its text or a chart label.
- `claim`: the finding in one sentence, with the numbers the code prints, and nothing the printout does not show: the story's own wording and numbers belong in `source`, not in the claim.
- `tables`: the files the code reads, each a variable name and the file's path from this folder, such as `data/orders.csv`; every file is read with `pd.read_csv(path)`.
- `code`: one Python expression over those variables, with `pd` (pandas) and `np` (numpy) available: the plain pandas computation whose printout shows the finding, such as a filter, a group-by, a count, a share or a sort. Do not assemble the result into a hand-made Series or dict.

Evaluate every fact from this folder the way it will be checked: read its `tables` with `pd.read_csv`, evaluate its `code`, print the value the way pandas prints it, and read the printout against the claim and the source. Every number, name and comparison in the claim must be in the printout, computed from the tables: code that writes a number itself, such as a string or a Series of typed-in values, does not count. The printout must agree with the story's numbers, up to rounding. Use the story's own definitions and filters, from its text or methods: a term means the same in every fact (if making it past the rookie contract is more than two seasons in one fact, it is more than two seasons in all of them), and a range, threshold or subset is one the story uses, never one chosen to make a number come out right. If the story's number only comes out under a definition or filter the story does not use, the finding is not reproduced. If after a fair try the data does not give the story's number (it needs other data, a different period, or the numbers differ beyond rounding), leave the finding out of facts.json.

4. Write `skipped.json`: every finding you left out, as [{"source": "the story's words", "why": "..."}].

Deliver both files, even when the data reproduces none of the story's findings: then `facts.json` is `[]`.
I'll start by exploring the data folder and reading the story.

What if you could search every visible word on New York City’s streets?
optometrist
51st
one way
abduction
Source: Google Street View, Aug 2011, 499 51st, Brooklyn
First, we’d need to transcribe every business sign, bumper sticker, ad, flyer—anything with text.
furniture
warehouse
optima
All these transcribed words are a wealth of information: non-English text could indicate a cultural enclave, like this one in Sunset Park, Brooklyn.
If you see something, say something
carniceria hispana
We can pinpoint the phrases that comprise NYC vernacular.
hardware
ups
lamps
From everyday common words…
Source: Google Street View, Jan 2018, 1173 2nd Avenue, Manhattan
…to phrases that uniquely blanket the city.
never forget
If you don't know, now, now you know
If you know, you know.
Source: Google Street View, Oct 2021, 2451 Victory Boulevard, Staten Island
This is possible because media artist
Yufeng Zhao
fed millions of publicly-available panoramas from Google Street View into a computer program that transcribes text within the images (
anyone
can access these Street View images; you don’t even need a Google account!).
The result is a
search engine
of much of what’s written in NYC’s streets. It's limited to what a Google Street View car can capture, so it excludes text in areas such as alleyways and parks, or any writing too small to be read by a moving vehicle.
The scale of the data is immense: over 8 million Google Street View images (from the past 18 years) and 138 million identified snippets of text.
So we can make frivolous things like this:
♬♫♩♪ New York...concrete jungle where dreams are made of...
‘Empire State of Mind’ by Alicia Keys &
Jay-Z
NYC’s Urban Textscape
Analyzing All of the Words Found on NYC Streets
Data by
. Story by
Matt Daniels
The data is astonishing; it feels like sifting through the city's source code. For example, here's all 111,290 matches for “pizza,” on a map.
View Images of “Pizza”
Let's look at some other maps.
The Geography of NYC Text
Broadway
62,424 matches
Matches for “Broadway” identify street signs, of course. The resulting map is oddly satisfying, illuminating each of the five boroughs’ Broadway.
View Images of “Broadway”
Zooming into Times Square, “Broadway” expands to depict Broadway theaters.
Luxury
16,731 matches
Every new residential building calls itself “luxury,” but only Hudson Yards has applied the label to an entire neighborhood.
View Images of “Luxury”
Beware
10,419 matches
There's a simple answer to why “beware” has such a clear geographic footprint, oddly completely absent from Manhattan. At the end of this article, we’ll show you why that is (or ask for a hint).
View hint!
View Images of “Beware”
Gold
51,353 matches
The map of “gold” depicts Manhattan’s Diamond District, as well as streets lined with “we buy gold” jewelry and pawn shops.
View Images of “Gold”
Iglesia
16,967 matches
Some of the more interesting maps depict cultural enclaves. Coordinates for “iglesia” (church, in Spanish) point to Spanish-speaking communities.
View Images of “Iglesia”
Jerk
4,900 matches
Similarly, “jerk” (the cooking style, not the personality) points to Jamaican enclaves in Flatbush, Brooklyn and Jamaica (the neighborhood), Queens.
View Images of “Jerk”
???
32,825 matches
See if you can guess this one, based on the geography: this adjective denotes that it’s not just a barbershop and not just a salon.
Submit

Title: NYC’s Urban Textscape
URL Source: https://pudding.cool/2025/07/street-view/
Published Time: Mon, 06 Jul 2026 15:03:34 GMT
Markdown Content:
[![Image 1](https://pudding.cool/2025/07/street-view/assets/branding/main.png)](https://pudding.cool/)
What if you could search every visible word on New York City’s streets?
Loading...Pls Wait!
Source: Google Street View, Aug 2011, 499 51st, Brooklyn
Source: Google Street View, Jan 2018, 1173 2nd Avenue, Manhattan
Source: Google Street View, Oct 2021, 2451 Victory Boulevard, Staten Island
This is possible because media artist [Yufeng Zhao](https://www.yufengzhao.com/) fed millions of publicly-available panoramas from Google Street View into a computer program that transcribes text within the images (_anyone_ can access these Street View images; you don’t even need a Google account!).
The result is a [search engine](https://alltext.nyc/) of much of what’s written in NYC’s streets. It's limited to what a Google Street View car can capture, so it excludes text in areas such as alleyways and parks, or any writing too small to be read by a moving vehicle.
The scale of the data is immense: over 8 million Google Street View images (from the past 18 years) and 138 million identified snippets of text.
So we can make frivolous things like this:
[Video 3](https://pudding.cool/2025/07/street-view/assets/images/NYCText.mp4)
♬♫♩♪ New York...concrete jungle where dreams are made of...
‘Empire State of Mind’ by Alicia Keys &Jay-Z
The data is astonishing; it feels like sifting through the city's source code. For example, here's all 111,290 matches for “pizza,” on a map.
![Image 2: Map of NYC showing the location of text that appears in Google Street View matching the phrase “pizza”](https://pudding.cool/2025/07/street-view/assets/images/pizza.jpg)
[View Images of “Pizza”](https://alltext.nyc/search?q=pizza)
Let's look at some other maps.
#### The Geography of NYC Text
Broadway 62,424 matches
Matches for “Broadway” identify street signs, of course. The resulting map is oddly satisfying, illuminating each of the five boroughs’ Broadway.[View Images of “Broadway”](https://alltext.nyc/search?q=Broadway)
![Image 3: Map of NYC showing the location of text that appears in Google Street View matching the phrase “Broadway”](https://pudding.cool/2025/07/street-view/assets/images/broadway.jpg)
Zooming into Times Square, “Broadway” expands to depict Broadway theaters.
![Image 4: Map of NYC showing the location of text that appears in Google Street View matching the phrase “”](https://pudding.cool/2025/07/street-view/assets/images/broadway-zoom.jpg)
Luxury 16,731 matches
Every new residential building calls itself “luxury,” but only Hudson Yards has applied the label to an entire neighborhood.[View Images of “Luxury”](https://alltext.nyc/search?q=Luxury)
![Image 5: Map of NYC showing the location of text that appears in Google Street View matching the phrase “Luxury”](https://pudding.cool/2025/07/street-view/assets/images/luxury.jpg)
Beware 10,419 matches
There's a simple answer to why “beware” has such a clear geographic footprint, oddly completely absent from Manhattan. At the end of this article, we’ll show you why that is (or ask for a hint).[View Images of “Beware”](https://alltext.nyc/search?q=Beware)
![Image 6: Map of NYC showing the location of text that appears in Google Street View matching the phrase “Beware”](https://pudding.cool/2025/07/street-view/assets/images/beware.jpg)
Gold 51,353 matches
The map of “gold” depicts Manhattan’s Diamond District, as well as streets lined with “we buy gold” jewelry and pawn shops.[View Images of “Gold”](https://alltext.nyc/search?q=Gold)
![Image 7: Map of NYC showing the location of text that appears in Google Street View matching the phrase “Gold”](https://pudding.cool/2025/07/street-view/assets/images/gold.jpg)
Iglesia 16,967 matches
Some of the more interesting maps depict cultural enclaves. Coordinates for “iglesia” (church, in Spanish) point to Spanish-speaking communities.[View Images of “Iglesia”](https://alltext.nyc/search?q=Iglesia)
![Image 8: Map of NYC showing the location of text that appears in Google Street View matching the phrase “Iglesia”](https://pudding.cool/2025/07/street-view/assets/images/iglesia.jpg)
Jerk 4,900 matches
Similarly, “jerk” (the cooking style, not the personality) points to Jamaican enclaves in Flatbush, Brooklyn and Jamaica (the neighborhood), Queens.[View Images of “Jerk”](https://alltext.nyc/search?q=Jerk)
![Image 9: Map of NYC showing the location of text that appears in Google Street View matching the phrase “Jerk”](https://pudding.cool/2025/07/street-view/assets/images/jerk.jpg)
???32,825 matches
See if you can guess this one, based on the geography: this adjective denotes that it’s not just a barbershop and not just a salon.
![Image 10: Map of NYC showing the location of text that appears in Google Street View matching the phrase “???”](https://pudding.cool/2025/07/street-view/assets/images/unisex.jpg)
A quick image search shows how these words appear on NYC streets. First, here’s a cliché Brooklyn phrase, which actually appears on signs as you exit the borough.
Fuhgeddaboudit
[![Image 11: Google Street View image of streetscape from ground level, viewing an example of “Fuhgeddaboudit” located at BQE, Verrazzano bridge, NYC](https://pudding.cool/2025/07/street-view/assets/images/fuhgeddaboudit_0.jpg)](https://maps.app.goo.gl/bYudE84yY6HNNbAy5)BQE, Verrazzano bridge[](https://maps.app.goo.gl/bYudE84yY6HNNbAy5)

The file is the ranked term-frequency table behind the story's two ranking charts. The key to the story's numbers is that the second chart is not the raw ranking: it is the ranking *after removing the terms flagged in the `street` column* (`street == '1'`). | Fedders #25 | 25th, 70,687 |
